subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.section_ref: Let's Take a Look Around Us!
periods.textbook_anchor: Let's Take a Look Around Us! — Draw a picture of your classroom and label the things drawn (p. 124)

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a pencil, a metal ruler, and a plastic bottle and asks: 'What are these objects? What are they made of?' Students share observations aloud, building a short class list on the board of objects and materials they already recognise.

Students open Textbook p. 124 and complete the activity: they draw a picture of their own classroom in their notebooks and label every object they include, naming what material it appears to be made of.

Students walk slowly around their own seats and look at Textbook p. 125 to guide a quick materials hunt — they list as many metal objects or parts as they can spot in the room and note the metal's name if they know it, or write 'ask elder' as a reminder.
Pairs share one surprising metal object they noticed. The teacher asks: 'Why do you think metal was used here instead of wood or plastic?' — collecting two or three ideas on the board to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe objects in their immediate environment and record what materials they are made of.
periods.section_context: Classroom objects (tables, chairs, windows, mats, bulbs, electric switches), metals identified in the classroom, Khushi's classroom drawing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Has anyone at home ever used an object made of a different material for the same job — like a clay pot instead of a metal vessel?' This draws out household diversity and intergenerational material knowledge naturally.

periods.textbook_anchor: See-through Materials! — Collect objects and look at a light source through them; order from most to least see-through (p. 126)
materials: assorted small objects: plastic bottle, glass bottle or jar, sheet of paper, piece of cloth, metal spoon or coin, candle or torch (teacher-held light source)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure on p. 126 showing the three categories

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds a glass jar and a metal spoon up to the window light. 'Can you see my hand through each of these?' Students predict and share. The teacher introduces the words transparent, translucent, and opaque on the board — one short example each.

Students open Textbook p. 126 and collect the objects they have on their desks (or share from a class set). Working in small groups, they hold each object up to the teacher-held torch or a candle and decide: can we see the light clearly, only partly, or not at all? They record each object in a three-column table in their notebooks labelled Transparent / Translucent / Opaque.

Groups order their tested objects from most to least see-through as the activity on Textbook p. 126 asks, writing the ordered list beneath their table. Each group tries to add at least one extra object from the classroom to their list.

Groups share their ordered lists. The teacher collates results on the board and asks: 'Did any two groups put the same object in different columns? Why might that happen?' — surfacing the idea that thickness and colour of a material can affect transparency.

periods.implied_lo: Students can sort materials by a physical property through a structured light-transmission test and record findings in a classified table.
periods.section_context: Plastic bottle, glass bottle or jar, paper, cloth, metal spoon tested against a light source; transparent, translucent, opaque categories.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do any of you have windows at home with coloured glass or frosted glass? What would you see through them?' — connecting the school activity to students' home environments.

periods.textbook_anchor: See-through Materials! — Look at white paper through coloured transparent materials and observe whether the colour appears to change (p. 127)
materials: coloured thin plastic bags or coloured plastic bottles (blue, yellow, red if available)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 127 illustration showing coloured see-through bags

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds a white sheet of paper, then covers it with a blue plastic bag. 'What colour does the paper look now?' Students predict before the teacher confirms. The class is told they will investigate this further using Textbook p. 127.

Students open Textbook p. 127 and, in pairs, look at a sheet of white paper through each coloured transparent material they have. They record what colour the paper appears to be through each material. They then try looking at a coloured object (e.g., a red eraser) through the yellow plastic and record what they see.

Pairs write two or three sentences in their notebooks answering the questions from Textbook p. 127: Does the white paper's colour appear to change? How did a blue object look through yellow plastic? They also note any experience they can recall of looking through coloured glass or a coloured plastic wrapper in daily life.

The teacher invites two or three pairs to share an experience they recalled. The class discusses: 'Where in everyday life do we use coloured transparent materials, and why might that be useful?' — closing with two or three student ideas.

periods.implied_lo: Students can investigate how a material's colour affects what is observed through it and connect the finding to everyday experience.
periods.section_context: Coloured thin plastic bags or bottles (blue, yellow), white paper, coloured objects viewed through coloured transparent materials.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students whether anyone has seen coloured glass in lamps at festivals or temples. This naturally surfaces cultural uses of coloured transparent materials without framing it as a separate topic.

periods.activity_title: Chain Game — Grouping Objects by Material
periods.textbook_anchor: What is it made of? — Complete the table grouping objects by material and add a new row for a material not in the list (p. 128)
materials: a metal spoon, a wooden ruler, a glass or plastic bottle, a piece of cloth — one set per group if available
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 128 table (wood, metal, glass, plastic columns)

time_bands.activity: The teacher briefly traces two familiar materials back to their source: 'The wood in your desk came from a tree. Where do you think glass comes from?' Students guess freely. The teacher introduces the idea that most materials come from something in nature — trees, rocks, sand — before being shaped by people.

Students open Textbook p. 128 and complete the chain-game table: they fill the third column with objects they know made from each material (wood, metal, glass, plastic). They then add an extra row for a material not in Khushi's list — the textbook suggests clay or rubber — writing the material name and objects made from it.

Groups of three share their completed tables. The class discusses: 'Which material did most people add in the extra row, and why do they think that material matters in daily life?' The teacher writes two or three student-named materials on the board and asks where each comes from in nature.

The teacher poses a closing question for students to think about before leaving: 'Ask an elder at home whether any household objects in your family are made from materials that are hard to find in shops now.' This sets up the intergenerational Find-out conversation.

periods.implied_lo: Students can group familiar objects by the material they are made from and trace those materials to a natural source.
periods.section_context: Wood, metal, glass, plastic objects; clay and rubber as additional materials; natural sources (trees, ore, sand); Khushi's grouping table.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In your grandparent's kitchen, what were pots and spoons made of? Is that the same today?' — drawing out the intergenerational material-change knowledge embedded in the section naturally.

periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Bend? — List five objects paired with unsuitable materials and explain why those materials will not work (p. 130)
materials: one metal spoon per pair or group

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up a piece of cloth and asks: 'Could we make a table out of this? Why not?' Then holds up a wooden stick: 'What about this? What is different?' Students name properties — hard, soft, rigid, bendy — and the teacher writes them on the board. The spoon from Textbook p. 129 is introduced as the starting object.

Students examine a metal spoon (Textbook p. 129 reference) and describe it using the words on the board: smooth or rough? Dull or shiny? Does it feel cold to the touch? They write their descriptions in their notebooks. The teacher then asks: 'Would a cloth spoon work? A paper spoon? A rubber table? A glass hammer?' — building the concept of unsuitable material pairings.

Students open Textbook p. 130 and complete the Odd Pairs writing activity: they list five objects and pair each with a clearly unsuitable material, then write a sentence for each pair explaining why that material will not work. The teacher circulates and prompts students to use the property words from the board (hard, soft, flexible, rigid, smooth).

Students share their most creative Odd Pair aloud. The class votes on the most surprising pairing. The teacher closes by connecting back: 'So the material chosen for an object depends on what properties it needs — this is why builders, weavers, and potters each choose their materials carefully.'

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why a material is or is not suitable for a given object by referring to its physical properties.
periods.section_context: Metal spoon (smooth, shiny, cold to touch, hard), cloth and wood compared for rigidity and flexibility, Odd Pairs activity with unsuitable material choices.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Can anyone name a craft or occupation where the choice of material is very important — like a potter choosing clay, or a weaver choosing cotton?' This surfaces cultural knowledge of material selection without labelling it separately.

periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Bend? — Tap a metal spoon on objects of different materials, describe the sounds in invented words, and compose beats (p. 130)
materials: five small objects made of different materials: wood block or ruler, metal tin or coin, plastic bottle or container, piece of cloth, small glass or ceramic cup

time_bands.activity: The teacher taps a metal spoon on the desk (wood) and a glass, asking: 'Do those sound the same?' Students listen and shake their heads. The teacher explains: the material an object is made of affects the sound it makes when tapped — today students will discover this for themselves.

Students open Textbook p. 130 and, in pairs, gently tap the metal spoon on each of their five objects in turn. For each, they invent a word that captures the sound — like ting-ting, dhum-dhum, dub-dub as the textbook suggests — and write it next to the object's name in their notebooks, noting the material as well.

Using the sound-words they collected, each pair composes a short beat sequence in their notebook — for example: ting-ting / dhum / dub-dub / ting — and practises tapping it out on their objects in order. Pairs may give their beat a name.

Two or three pairs perform their beat sequence for the class. After each, the teacher asks: 'Which material made that sound?' — reinforcing the connection between material and acoustic property. The class applauds each composition.

periods.implied_lo: Students can record observations about a material's properties using invented descriptive language and present findings through an expressive sequence.
periods.section_context: Metal spoon tapping wood, metal, plastic, cloth, glass or ceramic; invented sound words (ting-ting, dhum-dhum, dub-dub); student-composed beat sequences.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone heard a dhol, a thali, or a ghatam being played? What are those instruments made of, and how does that affect their sound?' — connecting the tapping investigation to familiar musical instruments without requiring prior knowledge.

periods.activity_title: Sorting Matter: Solid, Liquid, or Gas?
periods.textbook_anchor: Does it Flow? — Sort ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, and water into solid, liquid, and gas categories (p. 132)
materials: a small container of honey if available (or a picture)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 132 diagram of tray (solid), bottle (liquid), balloon (gas)

time_bands.activity: The teacher pours a small amount of water from a bottle into a cup, then tips the cup. 'What did the water do? Did the stone do the same thing?' Students observe. The teacher introduces the three categories — solid, liquid, gas — with one everyday example each, written on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 132 and work through the sorting activity: for each of the ten named objects (ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, water) they write the name in the correct column (tray / bottle / balloon) in their notebook. They then add at least two of their own examples to each column.

The teacher poses the edge-case challenge from Textbook p. 132: 'What about sand, sponge, or clay — are they solid, liquid, or a bit of both?' Students discuss in pairs, then share. The teacher records the puzzle objects on the board and helps students articulate why they are tricky.

Closing discussion: 'Can you think of a time in your day when you move from one state of matter to another — like ice melting in a drink, or steam from a hot pot?' Students give two or three examples. The teacher affirms that states of matter are part of everyday life.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify materials as solid, liquid, or gas based on whether they hold their shape, and identify edge cases that do not fit neatly.
periods.section_context: Ink, stone, smoke, ice, steam, spoon, honey, bottle, bag, water; tray/bottle/balloon sorting diagram; edge cases: sand, sponge, clay.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In your home, is water stored in a clay pot, a metal vessel, or a plastic container? Does the container change what state the water is in?' — connecting the states-of-matter concept to household storage practices.

periods.activity_title: Natural and Artificial: Listing and Seasonal Observation
periods.textbook_anchor: Natural — Artificial — List five natural and five artificial things and guess the season from a mango tree drawing (p. 133)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 133 illustration of Khushi's mango tree drawing

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a quick stick tree on the board and asks: 'Did anyone make this tree? Could I have made a real one?' Students recognise the difference. The teacher introduces the terms natural (found in nature, not made by people) and artificial (made by people) and asks for two or three quick examples of each.

Students open Textbook p. 133 and study Khushi's mango tree drawing. They discuss in pairs: 'Is a mango tree natural or artificial? What about a mango pickle jar? A wooden table?' The teacher steers the conversation to include non-living natural things: rocks, water, air.

Students complete the Textbook p. 133 writing activity: they list five natural things and five artificial things in their notebooks. They are encouraged to include at least one non-living natural example and at least one thing they found surprising to classify.

The teacher returns to Khushi's mango tree picture (Textbook p. 133) and poses the seasonal question: 'When do mangoes ripen — around January or around June? How do you know?' Students reason from their own experience of the mango season. The teacher closes by noting that natural things follow nature's timings, which people observe and depend on.

periods.implied_lo: Students can distinguish natural from artificial things and use observable natural evidence to make a reasoned seasonal inference.
periods.section_context: Mango tree (natural, living), rocks, water, air (natural, non-living), wooden table, clothes, shoes (artificial); Khushi's seasonal drawing; January vs. June mango season.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Are there seasonal fruits or flowers in your area that tell you what time of year it is? Which ones?' — inviting students to share local seasonal knowledge tied to natural cycles.

periods.activity_title: Reflection Drawing — Natural and Artificial Worlds
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw three natural and three artificial things (p. 134)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the four Let us reflect tasks from Textbook p. 134 and explains that this unit focuses on the drawing task and will also touch on the writing and discussion tasks. Students are reminded that their drawings should show understanding, not just artistic skill.

Students open Textbook p. 134 and complete the Draw task: they draw three natural things and three artificial things, labelling each clearly. The teacher encourages them to choose examples they have not already drawn in this chapter — stretching their recall across the chapter's content.

Students turn to the Write task on Textbook p. 134 and write the names of three materials they commonly see around them, then complete the matching activity (Textbook p. 134): they match transparent, translucent, and opaque to the three given examples (spectacle glass, lamp shade, plate).

The class discusses the Discuss task from Textbook p. 134: 'If you find a shining spoon and don't know whether it is metal or just painted to look shiny, how would you find out?' Students suggest tests — tap it, scratch gently, feel its temperature. The teacher lists the suggested tests and asks which property of metals each test relies on.

periods.implied_lo: Students can present their understanding of natural versus artificial things and material properties through drawing, writing, and oral reasoning.
periods.section_context: Three natural and three artificial things drawn; three common materials named; transparent/translucent/opaque matched to spectacle glass, lamp shade, plate; shining spoon identification discussion.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: As students draw, circulate and ask: 'Can you add one thing that your grandparent might have used at home that you do not commonly see today?' — inviting intergenerational memory into the creative task.

periods.activity_title: This World of Things — Whole-Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Discuss how to find out whether a shining spoon is metal or painted (p. 134)
materials: a plastic or wooden spoon (painted silver if possible, otherwise a clearly different material)
one small object per group from the classroom
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 134 Let us reflect questions

time_bands.activity: The teacher holds up both spoons — one metal, one painted plastic or wooden — and asks: 'These both look shiny. Are they the same material? How could you tell?' Students suggest tests freely. The teacher writes the suggested tests on the board without evaluating them yet, framing this as the chapter's big question.

The class revisits the chapter's main ideas together through teacher-led questions, not re-teaching: 'What three categories did we use when testing materials with light? What are the three states of matter? What is the difference between a natural thing and an artificial one? What makes a material suitable or unsuitable for a job?' Students answer from memory; the teacher confirms and adds any missed idea on the board. The chapter's concepts — transparency, hardness and flexibility, states of matter, natural vs. artificial, materials from nature — are now visible as a connected web on the board.

Each group receives one small object from the classroom. They apply as many of the chapter's classification tools as they can to that single object: What material is it made of? Where does that material come from in nature? Is the material transparent, translucent, or opaque? Is it hard or flexible? Is it solid, liquid, or gas? Is it natural or artificial? Groups record their findings in a short table in their notebooks.

Groups share one finding that surprised them. The teacher closes by returning to the two spoons: students vote on which tests from the board would best reveal the metal, and why — drawing on the properties of metals discussed across the chapter's material. The teacher notes that the same object can be examined through many lenses, and that is what the chapter has built.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply multiple material-classification frameworks — transparency, hardness, state of matter, natural versus artificial — to a single object and justify each classification.
periods.section_context: Metal spoon versus painted non-metal spoon; transparency/translucency/opacity; hardness and flexibility; solid/liquid/gas states; natural and artificial categories; materials and their natural sources.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which of these ideas about materials do you think someone in your family already knows — even without going to school — because of their craft, cooking, or work?' — honouring practical knowledge and connecting it to the chapter's scientific vocabulary.

assessment_items.question_text: Riya holds three objects up to a bright torch one at a time: a glass bottle, a piece of thick cardboard, and a thin white cloth. Which order correctly places them from MOST see-through to LEAST see-through?

options.label: A
options.text: Glass bottle → thick cardboard → thin white cloth

options.label: B
options.text: Glass bottle → thin white cloth → thick cardboard

options.label: C
options.text: Thick cardboard → glass bottle → thin white cloth

options.label: D
options.text: Thin white cloth → thick cardboard → glass bottle

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests ordering by degree of light transmission, which is the core skill of the light-transmission sorting activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can sort materials by a physical property through a structured light-transmission test and record findings in a classified table.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the order entirely, possibly confusing transparency with opacity — a foundational misconception about what 'see-through' means.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has correctly identified that cloth is not fully opaque but has overestimated its transparency relative to glass, confusing translucent with transparent.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has recognised glass as most transparent but confused the relative positions of cloth and cardboard, likely not recalling that cloth allows partial light transmission.

assessment_items.question_text: Anaya looks at a red eraser through a thin yellow plastic bag. She says the eraser looks a different colour. Why does the colour appear to change? Give one reason.
expected_elements: The yellow colour of the plastic mixes with or filters the light coming from the eraser, so the colour seen through it is different from the original colour.
The student connects the observation to the property of the transparent coloured material changing how the colour of objects appears (any equivalent explanation accepted).
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any response that explains the colour change by reference to the yellow material affecting the light or the colour seen. Do not require technical optical vocabulary.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can investigate how a material's colour affects what is observed through it and connect the finding to everyday experience.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: States that the yellow plastic changes or filters the colour of the light or the object seen through it.
Connects the change to the colour of the transparent material itself (yellow plastic causes the change, not the eraser).

assessment_items.question_text: Mohan's grandmother used to have a clay pot to store water. Today, Mohan's family uses a plastic container. What does this change tell us about materials over time?

options.label: A
options.text: Clay pots are no longer found anywhere in India.

options.label: B
options.text: Grandmother's pot was made of glass, not clay.

options.label: C
options.text: New materials such as plastic have replaced some traditional materials like clay for the same household use.

options.label: D
options.text: Plastic is always better than clay for storing water.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests whether the student has engaged with the intergenerational material-change discussion grounded in the 'What is it made of?' section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can group familiar objects by the material they are made from and trace those materials to a natural source.

competency.competency_text: Connects changes in the environment and the lives of their family and community, as communicated by elders and through local stories (changes in occupation, food habits, resources, celebrations, communication)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has over-generalised, incorrectly inferring that because one family switched materials, clay pots have disappeared entirely — a recall confusion with the chapter content.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has made a value judgement not supported by the chapter; the chapter describes change without declaring one material superior.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused materials; this is a recall error about what the chapter identifies as a traditional water-storage material.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya wants to make a chair. Her friend suggests making it from thick rubber instead of wood. Give TWO reasons why thick rubber would not be a good material for a chair.
expected_elements: Rubber is flexible / bendy / soft, so it would not hold the weight of a person sitting on it without collapsing or changing shape.
Rubber is not rigid / hard enough to keep the shape of a chair, whereas wood is hard and rigid and does not bend under weight.
assessment_items.annotation: Award one mark per correct property-based reason, up to two. Accept equivalent phrasing; the student must name a physical property (flexibility, softness, lack of rigidity) rather than a vague 'it won't work' answer.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why a material is or is not suitable for a given object by referring to its physical properties.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with disciplinary core ideas in the natural sciences, as well as in engineering, technology, and applications of science, which reflect the content that will be learned across subject areas in later Grades

expected_elements: Identifies that rubber is flexible or soft and therefore unsuitable for a weight-bearing structure.
Contrasts rubber with wood by noting that wood is hard and rigid, making it suitable where rubber is not.

assessment_items.task: You tapped a metal spoon on a wooden block and it made a dull 'dhum' sound. Then you tapped it on a glass cup and it made a ringing 'ting' sound. Draw or write a short beat using at least THREE different materials. Under each material, write the sound word it made.
format_of_output: A written or drawn beat sequence showing at least three materials and a sound word for each
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any three materials that the student has access to. Sound words are invented — there is no single correct answer. Assess whether the student has paired each material with a distinct sound word, showing awareness that different materials produce different sounds.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can record observations about a material's properties using invented descriptive language and present findings through an expressive sequence.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student shows that different materials produce different sounds when tapped, and can represent this observation through invented expressive language in a structured sequence.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold prompts three columns — material, sound word, beat position — helping students who struggle to organise their observations spontaneously. It is a support, not a constraint: students may add more than three materials.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: three distinct materials, three distinct sound words that are clearly different from each other, and a beat sequence that could actually be tapped out. Weak: repeated sound words for different materials, or a list of materials with no sound words.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may draw the objects and write only the sound word beneath each; students who have not seen all materials may substitute any classroom object they did tap. The beat may be written as a repeating pattern or a single line.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The activity's core learning is expressive observation — the format mirrors the textbook's own invitation to invent sound words and compose beats, making the output directly authentic to the activity.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at these four things: a stone, honey, steam, and a sponge. Which one is HARDEST to place in exactly one of the groups — solid, liquid, or gas?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item targets the edge-case reasoning from the states-of-matter sorting activity — sponge holds its shape like a solid but can be compressed and holds liquid like neither a pure solid nor a liquid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify materials as solid, liquid, or gas based on whether they hold their shape, and identify edge cases that do not fit neatly.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not engaged with the edge-case reasoning; stone is a straightforward solid and was not listed as a puzzle object in the sorting activity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be thinking of honey's slow flow as confusing, but honey clearly takes the shape of its container and is classified as a liquid — the student has not distinguished a slow liquid from an edge case.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may find steam puzzling (gas or water?), but steam as a gas was directly classified in the textbook activity; it is not the edge case the chapter highlighted.

assessment_items.question_text: Khushi sees a mango tree full of ripe mangoes outside her window. Which time of year is it most likely to be?

options.label: D
options.text: It could be any time of year because mangoes are always available in shops.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The item tests seasonal observation from the Natural–Artificial section. Regional variation: in some parts of India, early varieties ripen slightly earlier or later — accept March–July as a reasonable window if a student provides a written justification. D is a distractor testing whether the student conflates market availability with natural seasonality.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can distinguish natural from artificial things and use observable natural evidence to make a reasoned seasonal inference.

competency.competency_text: Observes and identifies the natural (insects, plants, birds, animals, geographical features, sun and moon, stars, planets, natural resources) and social (houses, relationships) components in their immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected mango ripening to the Indian summer season; January is a winter month when mangoes are not in season.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be thinking of a post-monsoon harvest but has not recalled the mango season; October is after the mango season in most of India.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused market availability (artificial distribution) with the natural cycle of ripening — a key confusion the Natural–Artificial section addresses.

assessment_items.task: Draw THREE natural things and THREE artificial things. Label each drawing with its name and whether it is natural or artificial.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Natural things: [space for three drawings with labels]
Artificial things: [space for three drawings with labels]
format_of_output: Six labelled drawings — three natural, three artificial — with natural/artificial label on each
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any six correctly classified examples. Watch for students who draw only living things as natural (missing rocks, water, air) or who classify raw materials (e.g., a tree trunk) as artificial. These are the two main classification errors to note and address.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can present their understanding of natural versus artificial things and material properties through drawing, writing, and oral reasoning.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can distinguish and represent the natural/artificial classification visually, showing understanding of the category boundary — including non-living natural things — not just living organisms.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates the two groups spatially so students do not mix categories. It is a layout aid; students are free to draw in any style.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: includes at least one non-living natural example (rock, water, air, soil) and one clearly artificial human-made object; labels are accurate. Weak: all natural drawings are plants or animals only (missing non-living natural things), or one or more items are misclassified.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may write the names of the things instead of drawing them. Students may choose examples from their home environment — local fruits, local crafts — all accepted.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Drawing is the format the textbook specifies for this reflection task and is appropriate for Grade III, allowing students who are stronger visually to demonstrate understanding without being blocked by writing difficulty.

assessment_items.question_text: You find a shiny spoon in your kitchen. You are not sure whether it is made of metal or whether it is made of plastic and painted to look shiny. Describe TWO different tests you would do to find out, and explain what result would tell you it is metal.
look_for: Names a physically reasonable test (e.g., tap it and listen for a ringing sound; feel whether it is cold to the touch; try to bend it; scratch it lightly).
For each test, explains what a metal result would look and feel like (e.g., metal feels cold, metal rings when tapped, metal does not bend easily, metal scratched shows a metallic colour underneath).
Uses at least one property vocabulary word from the chapter (hard, rigid, shiny, cold, smooth, ringing sound).
Response shows understanding that the test relies on a property of metals, not just 'look at it'.
assessment_items.annotation: Award marks for each clearly reasoned test-result pair. Do not penalise informal language. A student who names only one test but explains it well should receive partial credit. A student who says only 'it will look different' without naming a property has not met the standard.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply multiple material-classification frameworks — transparency, hardness, state of matter, natural versus artificial — to a single object and justify each classification.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

look_for: Identifies a testable physical property of metals (coldness, hardness, sound when tapped, appearance when scratched) rather than just describing how it looks.
Explains the expected result for a metal (e.g., 'if it rings when tapped, it is likely metal; plastic gives a dull sound') — showing understanding that the test has a predicted outcome.
Names at least two distinct tests, each based on a different property.
Uses chapter vocabulary (hard, rigid, smooth, shiny, cold to touch) at least once to anchor the reasoning in the chapter's content.
